newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel gives guarded support to French tax hike.
newsitem.headline: Waigel gives guarded support to French tax hike.

text.p: Germany gave a guarded welcome to France's decision on Monday to raise taxes to try and get closer to the borrowing targets required to join European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the tax increase might cause some economic pain for France, but should not be viewed as creative accounting to achieve a one-off fulfilment of the Maastricht treaty convergence criteria.

Waigel told reporters here that he had spoken with French counterpart Dominique Strauss-Kahn, who had said Paris wanted to meet the Maastricht budget deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product both in 1997 and 1998.
But he declined to venture an opinion on whether the French tax hikes would be enough to ensure a prompt start to EMU with both France and Germany on board.
"I think it would not be good if we gave an assessment of chances," Waigel told a news conference.

He added it was up to each country to evaluate its own prospects. "I will not participate in speculation here. From a political point of view, it is certain that monetary union without France or Germany makes little sense," he said.

Waigel was speaking after Strauss-Kahn hit businesses with 22 billion francs in higher taxes and announced a further 10 billion francs in spending cuts after an audit showed the French budget deficit running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of GDP.
"Less would have been insufficient, more would have blocked economic growth," Strauss-Kahn told reporters in Paris. He also said the 1998 budget would limit the deficit to three percent.

The tax hikes are intended to knock two-fifths of a percentage point off the French budget deficit, most probably leaving a small overshoot on the strict "3.0" interpretation of Maastricht stongly favoured by the German government.
"France believes it can cut its deficit by 0.4 percentage points (of GDP) through tax measures, and that it has potential for more savings through other measures," Waigel said.
He declined to give a forecast on the French deficit, but Bonn on Monday yet again reaffirmed its determination to hit the budget deficit target on the nose.
"Our goal is 3.0 percent and we will reach that," government spokesman Peter Hausmann told a news conference.

Asked to comment on France's chances of cutting government borrowing enough to meet the terms of the Maastricht treaty, Hausmann said: "What is important is that we all do our homework. It would be inappropriate to offer any advice."
Although government leaders refused to speculate on France's chances of making the grade for EMU, other politicians have urged the whole project to be put on ice because of Paris's budget woes.

Michael Glos, parliamentary party leader of Waigel's own Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), said at the weekend that a delay should be discussed if France's deficit exceeds 3.0 percent of GDP this year.
And a former government minister and elder statesman weighed in on Monday with much stronger language.
Otto Graf Lambsdorff said France would miss the deficit target by too much to take part in EMU. "If the numbers stay like this, then France is out," Lambsdorff told Saarland Radio.

Lambsdorff, a member of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats who served as Economics Minister from 1977 to 1984, said that with Paris was overshooting the deficit target "by too much" a delay to EMU would be "politically desirable".
